note: The most common way a surveyor states 1.40 m: unit FIRST, then the cm part as a bare tens word. Parser must read מטר as an implicit '1' integer part and ארבעים as 40 cm on top, not as a standalone 40 (which would trip the cm heuristic and yield 0.4/40).
'X וחצי מטר' pattern — number, then וחצי, then unit at the END. Danger: a substring matcher sees 'חצי מטר' and returns 0.5, ignoring the שניים. Word order matters: וחצי after a number adds 0.5 to it.
Leading filler word בערך ('roughly') that surveyors say constantly. Parser must skip it and still apply the חצי-BEFORE-מטר rule (=0.5, not 1.5). A parser that anchors to token position 0 fails.

Speaker said 'נקודה שמונים' (point eighty) with no leading zero; the recognizer normalized נקודה to a bare leading '.'. Sibling of the just-fixed 'אחד. ארבע חמש' bug: here there is NO integer part at all, so the parser must supply the implicit 0 and not concatenate שמונים=80 into 80 → cm heuristic.

Leading אפס. Parsers whose word tables start at 1, or that treat 0 as falsy/'no number found', drop the integer part or reject the whole utterance. Shallow inverts under 1 m are said exactly like this.

Variant of the exact field bug that was just fixed: recognizer glues the normalized decimal point to the preceding word ('שתיים.'), then two single-digit words that must CONCATENATE to 35 hundredths — not add to 8 (which would give 2.8, the same failure class as the 9 bug).

Feminine teen: אחת עשרה = 11 must stay ADDITIVE/compound. A concat-happy parser after the 'ארבע חמש'=45 fix may read אחת(1) עשרה(10) as digits and emit 110 or 1.10. Then the decimal part must still attach: 11.2.
Bare עשר (10) — many word tables only carry עשרה as a teen SUFFIX (שתים עשרה etc.), so standalone עשר misses or binds wrongly. Plus וחצי with the clitic ו must add 0.5, not start a new concatenation.

Fractional part spoken as a compound tens number ('forty-and-five') instead of digit-by-digit. Inside the fraction, ארבעים וחמש must resolve additively to 45 then be treated as hundredths; a digit-concat rule applied blindly gives .405, and a parser that only concatenates single digits after נקודה gives .4 and drops חמש.
Mixed gender mid-utterance: masculine ארבעה then feminine שתיים. Real speakers switch genders freely; a lookup table with only feminine forms (ארבע/שתיים) misses ארבעה and returns 0.2 or null.

Unit-first run-on for 1.25 m: מטר, then compound 25 with the ו clitic. Parser must treat the trailing compound as centimeters on top of the implicit 1 m — not as a standalone 25 that trips the cm heuristic into AMB 0.25|25.
Construct-state שני (not שניים) — the normal colloquial form before מטר. Unit in the MIDDLE with וחצי after it. Tables lacking שני parse this as 'מטר וחצי' = 1.5, silently losing a full meter.

Colloquial 'four twenty' = 4.20 m. One letter away from the teen ארבע עשרה (14): a teen-matcher that fuzzy-matches or an additive rule (4+20=24 → cm heuristic → 0.24) both fail. Digit-then-tens juxtaposition here means integer.decimal, not a compound integer.

Run-on 'one forty' = 1.40 m, said without מטר at all. Additive parse gives 41 → cm ambiguity (0.41|41); naive concat gives 140 → 1.40 which is accidentally right — so a test passing here may pass for the wrong reason. The intended semantics are digit=meters, tens=cm.

מאה עשרים must stay additive hundreds (100+20=120), never concat (10020 or 1.100...). Then the bare-integer>15 cm heuristic applies: offer 1.2 m (preferred, in range) and 120. A parser ranking by literal magnitude or skipping the heuristic on multi-word numbers returns only 120.

Google's Hebrew recognizer often normalizes the digits to numerals but leaves the decimal word נקודה untouched — half-normalized output. Parser must treat נקודה as the decimal point between digit chunks.

Recognizer converted נקודה to a literal '.' and glued it to the preceding word while emitting the fraction as digits. Word-integer + glued dot + digit-fraction is exactly the family of the field bug ('אחד. ארבע חמש' → 9).

A micro-pause before the last digit makes the recognizer close the number early and emit the final digit as a separate token. The trailing '5' must be concatenated onto the fraction (1.45), never added (1.4+5).
Each spoken fraction digit came out as its own numeral token. Consecutive single digits after the decimal word are digit concatenation → .45, not 4+5=9 hundredths or two numbers.
Speaker said 'אפס חמש'; recognizer merged it into the digit chunk '05' with a leading zero. Parser must keep the leading zero in the fraction (3.05), not parse 05 as integer 5 → 3.5.
Sentence-final period appended by the recognizer's auto-punctuation. A trailing '.' with nothing after it is spurious punctuation, not a second decimal point — must not break or shift the parse.

Auto-punctuation inserted '.' at the pause where the speaker said נקודה, then the fraction digits arrived as words. This is the exact fixed field bug shape with a different integer — regression guard against 4+5=9.
Recognizer renders centimeters as the abbreviation ס"מ with a gershayim character (U+05F4 or straight quote). Explicit cm unit → divide by 100 unambiguously, no cm-heuristic ambiguity.
מטר abbreviated to מ' with a geresh/apostrophe — common recognizer rendering. The apostrophe must be recognized as part of the meter unit, not as junk that invalidates the token.
Speaker used the plural מטרים; parser unit-stripping must match the plural form, not just מטר, or the unit word leaks into junk detection.
No digits at all — unit-first order means 1 + 0.5. Order matters: this is 1.5, while 'חצי מטר' would be 0.5. Recognizer outputs this verbatim since there is nothing to normalize.
Partial normalization again: the integer became a digit but the attached ו clitic on וחצי survives. Parser must strip the clitic and add the half → 1.5.

Surveyor answered in centimeters without saying the unit ('a hundred twenty'). Hundreds+tens stay additive (100+20=120), bare integer >15 with no decimal triggers the cm heuristic: offer 1.2 m (preferred) and 120.

Fully run-together token — digits fused directly onto the word נקודה with no whitespace, which Google's Hebrew output does when speech is fast. Tokenizer must split digit/letter boundaries before parsing.

transcript: העומק שתיים נקודה ארבע חמש בערך
note: Field speech includes filler/context words (העומק, בערך) around the number. Parser must extract the numeric span and ignore surrounding non-numeric words instead of returning null for 'junk present'.

Dual counted-noun form — 'two meters' with NO numeral word anywhere in the utterance. The most natural way any Palestinian speaker says 2 m. A parser that only maps digit-words and strips a متر unit token sees an unknown word and returns null. Known gap.

Dual + attached ونص clitic in one token. Parser must decode مترين=2 AND treat ونص as +0.5 after the unit, mirroring מטר וחצי. Failing the dual makes this 0.5 (only ونص recognized) — a 2 m error in the field.
Half BEFORE the unit = 0.5 m. Word-order test: same two content words as متر ونص but opposite meaning. An order-insensitive bag-of-words parser returns 1.5 here.
Unit-then-half = 1.5 m, the counterpart of the previous case. Also tests the attached و on نص; a tokenizer that splits ونص into و + نص must not treat و as an additive conjunction over nothing.

Levantine تنين for 'two' (recognizers emit it instead of اثنين), additive units-and-tens order (two-and-twenty = 22), explicit سم so /100 is unambiguous. A parser trained only on MSA اثنين drops the 2 and returns 0.20.
MSA decimal word فاصلة with two consecutive single-digit words after it — must CONCATENATE to .45, never add to .9. Arabic twin of the Hebrew field bug that shipped 1.9 instead of 1.45.

Recognizer normalized فاصلة to a literal '.' glued to the preceding word — exactly the אחד. ארבע חמש failure mode that just got fixed for Hebrew. Verifies the fix also covers the Arabic pipeline; regression here silently reintroduces 9-style sums.

All-colloquial urban Palestinian: اتنين (not اثنين/تنين), تلاتة (not ثلاثة), and نقطة ('point') as the decimal word instead of فاصلة. Surveyors who learned decimals in Hebrew/English contexts say نقطة constantly; if only فاصلة is mapped this parses as garbage or as 23.

Eastern-Arabic digits with the ٫ (U+066B) decimal separator plus a trailing unit. Some Android keyboards/recognizers emit these on ar-locale devices; ٫ is visually a comma-like mark and naive Number() parsing yields NaN or 245.

Colloquial مية for 'hundred' (MSA مائة/مئة) + tens clitic → 150, bare integer >15 with no unit → cm heuristic must offer 1.5 (preferred) and 150. If مية is not in the lexicon the parser sees only خمسين=50 → wrong AMB:0.5|50.
Quarter after unit: 1.25 m, very common for shallow laterals. Tests that ربع=0.25 exists alongside نص=0.5 and combines additively with the unit rather than being read as 0.25 alone.

Counted-noun plural: numbers 3–10 take the plural أمتار, not متر. Unit-stripping that only matches متر/سم leaves أمتار as a trailing junk token and may null out an otherwise clean reading. Colloquial تلاتة doubles the trap.

Recognizer inserts و between the two single fraction digits (speakers do say it: 'أربعة وخمسة'). The و clitic must NOT flip concatenation into addition — the additive rule is for tens/hundreds only. Wrong answer is 1.9, the exact bug class just fixed.

Bare units-and-tens with attached و: five-and-forty = 45 (additive, NOT concatenation to 545). No decimal, no unit, >15 → cm heuristic offers 0.45 preferred plus 45. Distinguishing this additive pattern from the digit-concatenation pattern in case 6 is the core Arabic-numeral ambiguity.

Mixed register in one utterance: formal MSA اثنان (recognizer language models love it) followed by colloquial oblique أربعين. The tens-word AFTER the decimal must resolve additively to 45 then become the fraction .45 — concatenating word-by-word gives .545 or .5405, and dropping the MSA اثنان loses the integer part entirely.

Pure Eastern-Arabic numerals with U+066B arabic decimal separator (٫) — the canonical output of Android Arabic ASR when locale digit shaping is on; parser must map ٢→2, ٤→4, ٥→5 and treat ٫ as the decimal point.

Mixed-script artifact: recognizer emits the integer part in Eastern digits but falls back to ASCII dot and Western digits for the fraction — happens when the ASR language model switches mid-token. Both digit systems must normalize to one number.

Digits mixed with the spelled-out separator word فاصلة (comma) — Arabic speakers say فاصلة for the decimal point and the recognizer sometimes keeps it as a word between digit tokens instead of normalizing to ٫ or '.'.

All-words form with orthographic chaos: hamza-below alef in إثنين, hamza-less اربعه, and ta-marbuta→ha substitutions (فاصله/اربعه/خمسه) — extremely common in ASR output. Fraction digits اربعه خمسه must CONCATENATE to 45, not add to 9.

The Arabic twin of the field bug: recognizer normalized spoken فاصلة to a literal '.' glued to واحد. Must parse as 1.45 — the pre-fix parser dropped the dot and concatenated/added everything, yielding a wrong depth.

Two consecutive single-digit words = digit concatenation → 45 (never 4+5=9). Bare integer >15 with no decimal or unit triggers the cm heuristic: offer 0.45 (preferred, cm reading) and 45. Also exercises hamza-on-alef أربعة.
Arabic says units-before-tens: خمسة وستين = 5-and-60 = 65 (additive, not concatenation), with the و clitic attached to ستين. Explicit سم unit divides by 100 unambiguously → 0.65, no AMB.

Tatweel (U+0640 kashida) stretching inside متر — some recognizers/keyboards inject it; must be stripped before unit matching. نص is the colloquial Levantine/Egyptian form of نصف (half); متر ونص = meter-and-a-half = 1.5 (word order: unit first).

Fully diacritized output (kasra/sukun/fatha/damma) — MSA-mode recognizers sometimes emit harakat. Diacritics U+064B–U+0652 must be stripped so مِتْر matches متر and رُبْع matches ربع → meter and a quarter = 1.25.
Word-order test: half BEFORE the unit means half-a-meter = 0.5, the mirror of متر ونص = 1.5. Colloquial نص again instead of نصف.

ASR glues the coordinating و onto the following unit token, producing the non-word وسم instead of و + سم (speaker said أربعين سم with a filler). Parser must peel the و clitic off وسم to recover the cm unit → 40 cm = 0.40.
Colloquial dialect number: اتنين (Egyptian/Levantine for اثنين, with plain alef and dropped tha) — dialect ASR models output this constantly. Number + ونص + trailing unit = 2.5.
Colloquial مية for مائة/مئة (hundred). Hundreds+tens stay additive: 100+50 = 150. No unit, no decimal, integer >15 → cm heuristic offers 1.5 (preferred, in the 0-15 m depth range) and 150.

Teen/compound boundary case: خمسة عشر is the teen construction 15 (additive), NOT concatenation of خمسة=5 and عشر → '510' or 5+10 misreads. Exactly 15 is the top of the valid depth range, so no cm ambiguity fires (heuristic is >15).
Pure conversational junk ('okay, let's continue') captured when the mic stayed open — contains no number, half/quarter, or unit words; parser must return null rather than hallucinate a depth.

L2 speakers drop the decimal word: 'one forty five' means 1.45 m. Parser sees 1 then 45; concatenation yields 145 with no decimal and no unit, so the bare-integer>15 cm heuristic fires: offer 1.45 (in-range, preferred) and 145. Must NOT be additive (1+45=46).
Classic field dictation 'meter + remainder': the meter unit splits the utterance — 1 is whole meters, trailing 45 is centimeters. Unambiguous 1.45, no AMB flag, unlike case without the unit word.
'and a half' after an integer adds 0.5 (English analog of 'מטר וחצי'). The 'and' must not trigger the clitic-concatenation path (2 glued with 5 would give 25 or 2+half misread).
Decimal word with no leading integer — parser must supply the implicit leading zero. Recognizers often emit this when the speaker starts with the fraction. Returning 5 or null would be wrong.
Recognizers transcribe spoken zero as 'oh'. 'oh' must map to 0 before the decimal, not be treated as junk (which would demote to bare 'point five') or as an interjection that nulls the parse.
'oh' inside the fractional part is a placeholder zero digit. Fractional digits are positional concatenation: o-h five = 05, so 1.05 — not 1.5 (dropping the oh) and not 1.005.

English analog of the spec's 'מאה חמישים' example. 'a' acts as 1, hundred is multiplicative, 'and fifty' additive → 150; bare integer >15 with no decimal → cm heuristic offers 1.5 (preferred) and 150.
Digits with the meter unit glued directly to the number, no space — recognizers concatenate. Tokenizer must strip the trailing 'm' unit rather than fail the numeric match or read '45m' as junk.
Digit form of 'one meter forty five' with abbreviated unit between the numbers. The unit token splits meters from the cm remainder → 1.45. Must not concatenate to 145 or return only 1.

Teen word, value 13 ≤ 15 → a legal depth in range, so NO cm-heuristic ambiguity: return 13 alone. Guards against the parser confusing teen morphology with tens ('thirty') and against over-applying the /100 heuristic.

Tens word, value 30 > 15, bare integer, no decimal, no unit → cm heuristic fires: offer 0.3 (in-range, preferred) and 30. Paired with 'thirteen' to catch teen/ten misclassification — ASR confuses these constantly.

Digit-by-digit reading (very common for L2 speakers avoiding English number grammar). Single-digit words concatenate → 145, never 1+4+5=10. 145 m is out of range even with explicit 'meters', and in-range readings rank first, so 1.45 is preferred with 145 kept as the literal alternative.

English twin of the exact field bug just fixed ('אחד. ארבע חמס' → 9): recognizer normalizes spoken 'point' to a literal '.' glued to the preceding word. Must split 'one.' into 1 + decimal marker, then concatenate fractional digits 4,5 → 1.45 — never sum to 9 or 10.

Explicit cm unit is unambiguous: 45/100 = 0.45 with no AMB flag and no alternative 45 offered. Also re-checks tens+units concatenation (forty five = 45, not 4 5 → 45 by accident of a different code path).

Unit-first with trailing half and NO explicit numeral — 'meter' implies 1, 'and a half' adds 0.5 → 1.5 (analog of 'מטר וחצי'). Word order matters: this must not collapse into the 'half a meter'=0.5 branch.

Exact cm-heuristic threshold. The rule is 'bare integer >15' — 15 itself is a legal depth and must NOT be split into AMB 0.15|15. Off-by-one here (>= instead of >) would make the deepest legal integer depth ambiguous.

First integer past the threshold, as an English number word rather than digits. Verifies the heuristic fires on word-parsed values too (not only digit transcripts) and that n/100=0.16 is ranked first because it is in the 0-15 range.

Lower range edge as a word. Zero is falsy — any `if (value)` guard in the pipeline silently turns a real 0 m reading into null. Also must not trigger the cm heuristic (0 is not >15) or be rejected as 'no number found'.

Multi-dot: recognizers that normalize every spoken נקודה to '.' will emit this for 'אחת נקודה ארבע נקודה חמש' (surveyor spelling digits with redundant 'point'). parseFloat would silently give 1.4, dropping the 5 — the same digit-loss shape as the אחד. ארבע חמש bug. My pick: treat the first dot as THE decimal point and concatenate everything after it (1.45). NULL is defensible if you consider it malformed, but 1.4 must never be returned.
Degenerate: only the normalized decimal mark, no digits either side. parseFloat('.') is NaN but a naive split-on-dot yields ['',''] and can fabricate 0.0 or crash. Must be clean null, not '0'.

Bare unit, no number. Tension: 'מטר וחצי'=1.5 implies an implicit מטר=1, so returning 1 is arguably consistent. My pick is NULL: a lone 'מטר' in the field is almost always a truncated utterance (audio cut before the number), and inventing 1.00 m writes a plausible-looking wrong depth into a survey record — silent data corruption is worse than a re-prompt.

Bare 'and-a-half' with the ו clitic. The clitic grammatically marks a continuation of a missing head — it could complete 'מטר וחצי' (1.5), 'שניים וחצי' (2.5), anything. My pick is NULL (fragment, re-prompt); 0.5 is defensible only if you assume the lost head was מטר. Whatever the choice, it must not throw when the half-handler finds no base number.

Negative-sounding phrase. A parser that skips unknown tokens sees 'two meters' and returns 2.00 — a real depth fabricated from a phrase the speaker negated (e.g. reporting an elevation delta, or 'minus' as recognizer garbage). Sign words should poison the parse, not be ignored.

Huge additive number: 900+90+9 with the ו clitic on תשע. Stresses that hundreds/tens stay ADDITIVE (must not concatenate 9,90,9 into 9909 or 9-9-9 into 999 by the digit-concat path — same digit answer here but wrong mechanism elsewhere). 999/100=9.99 is in range so it is offered first; raw 999 kept as the marked-ambiguous alternative.

Hebrew dual form for 200 — a single irregular lexeme, not 'שתיים מאות', so it needs its own dictionary entry. Bare integer >15 with no decimal → cm heuristic offers 2.00 (in range, preferred) plus 200. Returning only 200, or failing to recognize the dual and returning null, are both plausible bugs.

Lone decimal word that the recognizer did NOT normalize to '.'. The word-number path must treat it like the lone-dot case: no integer part, no fraction, no value. A table that maps נקודה→'.' then parses could fabricate 0.

Eastern-Arabic digits for 16 WITH explicit cm unit. Deliberate contrast to bare 'sixteen': the unit resolves the ambiguity, so this must be a single unambiguous 0.16 — the cm heuristic must not fire and re-offer 16. Also checks ١٦→16 digit mapping before the unit division.

Leading Eastern-Arabic decimal separator with no integer part — recognizer output for 'فاصلة أربعة خمسة' (speaker omits the zero, common in field speech). Must parse as 0.45, symmetric with English '.45'; a tokenizer that requires digits before ٫ returns null or, worse, concatenates ٤٥ into the AMB 45-cm path (0.45|45) instead of the exact 0.45.

The mirror edge of the just-fixed 'אחד. ארבע חמש' bug: dot glued to the word but with NOTHING after it (audio cut after 'נקודה'). The glued-dot splitter now produces an empty fraction part — must yield 1, not null, not crash, and definitely not resurrect any additive path. Direct regression neighbor of the field bug.

Teen form 15 (additive עשרה, must not concat to 5-10) plus a decimal pushing it just past the 15.00 range edge. Spec only says in-range readings RANK above out-of-range ones — it never says reject. My pick: return 15.1 and let form validation flag it, because a surveyor in a genuinely 15.1 m structure should see their number, not a mysterious null. NULL is defensible if the 0-15 range is a hard invariant of the schema.
